result.process_description:
A guest enters the restaurant when feeling hungry. 
He chooses a dish from the changing meal range and waits until it is his turn. 
Following this he places his order with the employee. The employee enters the order into the POS system and collects the money from the guest. 
After the payment, the employee sets up a buzzer and passes it on to the guest with the following information: 
"When the buzzer rings, your dinner is ready". 
Afterwards the employee informs the chef of the new meal order. 
The chef prepares the meal and places it in the service hatch. 
He then informs the employee that he has placed the finished meal in the service hatch. 
As soon as the employee is aware that the meal is ready he sets off the guest's buzzer. 
This is how the guest finds out that his meal is ready for collection. 
He can pick up his meal and eat it. 
As soon as the guest appears at the service hatch, the employee hands over his meal. 
Should a guest not react to the buzzer, the employee calls for him after 5 minutes, if necessary several times in a row.

args.text: the description has one participant informing, handing over to, or calling another participant; model each participant as its own pool and connect the cross-participant handoffs with message flows instead of lanes or sequence flows

trace.reason: Check whether documented guidelines already cover pools versus lanes and message flows for interactions between participants before writing the guideline.

result.rule: Sequence flows may cross lanes in one process. Use message flows across participant pools, never between lanes.
Do not create separate pools for ordinary internal roles unless the description treats them as independent communicating participants.
Direct each message flow from sender to receiver. Its endpoints must belong to different pools and be valid interaction nodes.
Create bpmn:collaboration when distinct participants interact and represent every participant as a bpmn:participant pool.
Use sequence flows inside one participant process and message flows between different participants. Never use sequence flow across pools.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.

args.text: the description has a role that works in a separate place and exchanges messages with another role, such as informing, handing over or calling, so model that role as its own pool and connect the exchanges with message flows, not as a lane

trace.reason: Check whether error-driven guidelines already cover the lane-versus-pool choice for a separately located communicating role.

result.rule: When the description has a step of one role whose result is passed to a different role, and the receiving role then performs its own described step as a task in its own pool (for example, a role that is asked to act on information or an item another role has sent): Model the receiving step as a task in the receiving role's pool and draw a message flow from the sending step in the sender's pool to that receiving task, with the arrow pointing from sender to receiver. Do not replace this flow with one that ends at a catch event when the receiver's described step is a performed task, and do not reverse the arrow direction.

When the description is written in the first person as the account of one performing role that carries out the process's own steps, and the other parties it mentions (such as the party it sends requests to or receives replies from) are never described as having modeled steps of their own: Model the performing role as its own bpmn:participant pool inside a bpmn:collaboration, and place all of the process's start and end events, tasks, gateways and intermediate events in that pool. Do not create a pool for the other parties mentioned, and do not draw message flows to or from them unless the description states a message exchange. Model any reply the process must wait for as an intermediate catch event or event-based gateway inside the performer's pool.

When the description mentions an outside party only as the recipient of a request the company sends, or as the target of a case the company hands over, and never describes that party's own actions as a process participant: Do not create a pool for that outside party and do not draw message flows to or from it. Model the sending of the request or the handover as a task in the company's own process, and model any awaited reply as an intermediate catch event or event-based gateway in that same process.

When The description names several distinct kinds of outgoing communication sent to the same party within one stated activity, joined by commas or 'or' (for example, different notice or update types), and does not say they are alternatives in a decision.: Model each named kind of communication as its own send task within the activity, rather than merging them into a single task labelled with all the kinds. Connect these tasks with sequence flows or a gateway that reflects the stated relationship between them, and do not collapse them into one generic send task.
